Synthesises detail in the upscaler's output, before frame generation sees it.

  nvngx_dlssnr.dll       NVIDIA's model (~165 MB) -- you supply it

Undocumented and driven directly, so none of this is officially supported.
Can be toggled with a key -- bind it under Keybinds, "Neural Rendering".

Whether the model's edit is applied. Off shows the clean upscaler frame while the
pass keeps running -- so with Hold frame (under Compare) you can freeze a
frame and toggle this to see the same frozen frame with and without Neural
Rendering. Leave it on for normal use.
Off. The model stays loaded, so turning this back on is immediate.
Waiting for the upscaler to run.

Supersampling %.2fx: the model runs ABOVE native, then
is sampled back down. Experimental, and costly -- time grows with the area.

The filter that averages the model's above-native answer back to display size --
this is what turns supersampling into LESS noise rather than more. Sharper
filters (Lanczos3, Kaiser3) keep the most detail; softer ones (Bicubic,
Catmull-Rom) are gentler on ringing. Independent of the Output Scaling
downscaler, so the two can differ and run at the same time.

What fraction of the frame the model works at. Cost falls with the square of
this, so half resolution is roughly a quarter of the time.

The frame is never reduced. Only the model's contribution is computed small
and enlarged, so the picture underneath is untouched whatever this says.

What it trades: the shading the model adds is broad and survives enlargement;
the fine structure it synthesises does not, and softens. Worth having when the
pass costs more than you want to pay for the detail it returns.

The frame itself stays at full detail whatever this says -- only the
model's own work is done small.

How the model's work is brought back up when it ran below the frame's size.

Classic composes the model's small picture directly against the full-size
frame. Those two disagree by the shrink's blur as well as by the model's edit,
and the composition cannot tell them apart -- it reads the blur as brightness
the frame has and the model never saw. The lower the model resolution the
larger that error, and it is the colour shift that shows up at 50%.

Matched residual carries up only the model's difference and lays it on the
frame's own proxy, so both pictures being compared are full size and the only
thing that came from the small raster is the edit itself.

No effect at 100% or above: there is no residual to carry and the two are
identical (supersampling brings its answer down to frame size before this).

From hhkbble's multi-pass work on this fork.

How far the frame moves toward the model's picture.

The model's answer is not added to the frame -- it is a complete picture of its
own, rescaled so its luminance sits where the original says it should. This
blends between the two, so both ends are real pictures and everything between
them is one too.

0 gives back exactly what the upscaler produced. 1 is the model's picture.

Above 1 carries on past it in the same direction, which is not something the
model asked for -- use it to see what it is doing, then come back down. This
is the control to push if you want more effect: Intensity belongs to the model
and it decides what to do with it.

Whether the model's colour arrives with its light.

0 keeps the game's own hue exactly -- every pixel is the original colour with
only its brightness carrying the model's verdict. Game-accurate colour, with
the detail. 1 brings the model's colour as well, in its own hue, clamped into
AP1 so nothing unreachable is asked for.

This cannot shift hue on its own: it interpolates between two finished
pictures rather than adding a colour difference to one, which is what used to
let a warm subject come back green.

Above 1 it OVER-SATURATES: the colour keeps its hue but grows more vivid,
and rolls off at the edge of what the display can show rather than clipping
into a flat blown patch. 1 is the model's own colour; push past it for punch.

What the model is shown, and how its answer comes back.

Off (soft knee): the default. It rolls highlights off so hard the model
cannot resolve detail in them -- fine in soft-lit scenes, weak in bright ones.

Neutwo composed: an unclipped curve so the model sees highlight detail, then
everything above (Detail/Colour strength, highlight guard, palette). It wins in
bright scenes, but the curve compresses MIDTONES too, so in soft-lit content it
can be worse than Off. It also shifts paper white -- re-check it when you switch.

Hybrid composed: the best of both, and the one to use. Identity in the
midtones -- as good as Off there -- and the unclipped roll only in the
highlights, so it recovers the detail Off crushes without giving up the
midtones Neutwo does. It barely shifts paper white.

Replace: the raw model straight back through the exact inverse, none of the
composition -- no guard, no palette, no strengths. Gorgeous where there are no
bright lights, but they FLASH in motion. A reference, not a daily setting.

Hybrid replace: the raw model like Replace, but on the hybrid curve -- the
decode is identity in the midtones, so the flashing is confined to genuine
bright highlights instead of everywhere. Most of Replace's detail, far more
stable. If you love the Replace look but the flicker bothers you, use this.

Off is byte-identical to before.
Read when the model is built, so a change rebuilds it after a moment.

Default leaves the choice to the model.

Not the same scale as the super resolution or ray reconstruction presets --
the same number means something different here.

The model's own processing profiles.

Default (standard): the strongest. Boosts local contrast and deepens
lighting, and can oversaturate or look stylised -- most of what reads as
'the model changed my game's look' is this profile.

Natural: the same detail work with a gentler hand. Keeps skin tones and
tonal balance closer to what the game rendered.

Cinematic: tones down the shine and over-processing for a film-like look.

Read when the model is built, so a change rebuilds it after a moment. The
names come from community testing; NVIDIA ships no names in the binaries.

The model's own strength control, applied inside it. Distinct from detail
strength above, which scales the result afterwards.

-1 means follow local structure, and is the model's own default -- it is not a
strength of zero. 0 and above set skin independently of the rest of the frame.
Lets the model find skin itself rather than treating the frame uniformly.

The model was trained on finished, sRGB-encoded frames. The upscaler's
output is not one: it is linear and open-ended. These decide how it is
mapped into something the model recognises. A frame the game reports as
already tone-mapped is passed over untouched and none of this applies.

Where the number that divides the frame comes from.

Paper white only -- the slider below and nothing else. Right for a
game whose exposure never moves, wrong the moment it does: one
constant cannot serve a cave and a field.

The game's own exposure -- read from the texture the game hands
the upscaler. The best source there is, because it is decided
upstream and nothing this pass does can move it. Not every game
supplies one.

A buffer the scan found -- for games that compute an exposure and
never pass it on. A GUESS: candidates are matched by shape, and in
GTA V the best one tracks the real exposure but at its own scale,
which the anchor's ratio cancels. Needs anchoring once, and checking
afterwards.

The white point for the selected calibration point, or -- with no row
selected -- the value the next Anchor press captures.

Set it until the picture looks right here, then Anchor. Move to very
different light and do it again: two points fix the buffer's real
relationship and the white point holds between them. Click a row below
to come back and adjust that point; click it again to let go.

A multiplier on the scan's white point, and the control you adjust between
anchor points: dial it until the picture looks right in the current
light, then press Anchor here -- it captures the trimmed value as a new
point and resets the trim to 1.

A multiplier on the exposure the game supplied. 1.00x takes its number
exactly, and that is the right answer here.

This is not a fudge factor. If a game needs the trim far from 1 to look
right, that is evidence the exposure being read is wrong for that game,
not that the game wants trimming. Somewhere around 0.8 to 1.25 is honest
tuning; reaching for 4 means something upstream is broken and the trim is
hiding it.

Your manual paper white is kept separately and comes back untouched if
you switch the option above off.

What the frame is divided by before the model sees it. There is no other white
point; this is the whole of it.

The model was trained on finished frames where white sits at 1. The
upscaler's output is linear and open-ended, so something has to say where
white is -- and where the game's DLSS buffer is linear HDR, that number is
rarely anywhere near 1. Measured in Monster Hunter Wilds it takes 16 or more
before the model's detail reaches the frame at all, and the value that suits
a shaded camp is still too small for the same game out in daylight.

Too low and almost every pixel trips the soft knee: the model is shown a
flat near-white picture, its answer is scaled away, and only its hue
survives -- which reads as a colour cast rather than as lost detail. Too
high and it is shown an underexposed one, its answer degrades, and this same
number multiplies that error on the way out.

Raise it until the picture stops improving. Past that point it does not
plateau, it gets worse in the other direction.

This was once a multiplier on a measured white point. The measurement is
gone: it read scene brightness rather than where white belongs, handed the
model a picture three times too dark, and left the highlight path nothing to
give back.

At strength zero the frame is still bit-identical whatever this says.

The most the pass may move any pixel, as a multiple of what it already was, in
both directions -- a pixel may not be brightened past this nor darkened past
its reciprocal. Lights are where the model has least to say and rescaling its
answer does the most damage; 2x leaves detail intact while stopping a strip
light turning into a string of coloured cells. Raise it only if bright areas
look clipped.
Show the light meter on screen

A lamp in the corner: red for dark, green for full light, and the
shades between, with the reading beside it.

It is how you see at a glance that the scan is TRACKING rather
than merely running. Walk into shade and it should slide toward
red; step out and it should go green. If it moves the wrong way,
that is what the setting above is for.

Purely a readout. It changes nothing.

Make the picture look right, then press this -- it captures the current look
as a point. For the first point use the Paper white slider above; for
every point after, move to different light and use the Trim, which the
Anchor then bakes into a new point.

The first press calibrates one point -- the white point then
follows the scan by ratio from there, as before. Walk into very
different light, set paper white again, and press it again: the
second point pins down the buffer's real curve and everything
between the two is right, not just near one anchor. Up to eight.

The table is per game and shareable: one person calibrates a game
and the numbers are the same for everyone who takes the profile.
(the scan is only watching -- the white point above comes from somewhere else)
Click a row to edit it with the slider above; click it again to control the live point. > is the point in use now.
The number runs the other way

Flip this if the picture gets worse in the direction it should be
getting better. Most engines store an exposure that falls as
the scene brightens; some store its reciprocal, and a buffer
found by shape does not say which. Add a second anchor point in
different light and this is decided for you, so it disappears.
Walk from shade into daylight. A real exposure moves.
One that only ever climbs is a counter, not an exposure.

Freezes the frame the model works on. While held, change paper white, the
strengths, the reversible mode, the model preset -- anything below the
upscaler -- and only that setting moves; the scene does not.

What it CANNOT show: DLSS/FSR/XeSS upscaler presets or anything upstream
(the upscaler is not re-run on a held frame), and the game's own HUD and
post-processing, which run after this pass and keep updating. The white
point stops being measured and holds its value while frozen, so it cannot
drift and confound the comparison.

Hide the menu and it stays held. Untoggle to resume.

Shows the pass against itself, so the two can be seen at once rather than
toggled and remembered.

Side by side puts the whole frame in each half, untouched on the left and
edited on the right. Both halves are squeezed horizontally to fit, so it is
for looking at rather than playing in.

Wipe cuts a single frame at the split and resamples nothing, so the picture
is the right shape and can be played normally. Drag the split below; it is a
stored setting and stays put once the menu is closed.

Neither needs the menu open to keep working. A hairline marks the join.

Writes which side is which onto the frame itself, so a screenshot still
says so after it has left this machine. Drawn into the picture's own
plane: in the wipe the split reveals and hides the label exactly as it
does the images, and there is nothing to drag. Swap sides moves the
labels with their pictures.

Puts the edited frame on the other side.

Worth doing once you have decided which you prefer: the eye is not
even-handed about left and right, and a difference can read as an
improvement purely from where it sits. If the same side still wins after
swapping, it is the pass you are seeing and not the placement.

How much of the frame each half shows.

A half is half as wide as the frame and just as tall, so the frame
cannot fill it and keep its shape.

At 1 the whole frame is there at its right proportions, with bars above
and below. At 2 the half is filled and the sides are cropped away
instead. Anything between trades one for the other.

Where the wipe cuts. Left of it is the frame as the upscaler produced it,
right of it is the frame the model edited.

Proxy is the picture handed to the model -- if that looks wrong, the white point
is wrong and nothing downstream can be judged.

Difference shows what the model actually changed, amplified twenty times and
centred on grey. A flat grey frame there means it is doing nothing.
